planting.note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring or fall against a fence, arbor, or mailbox post in full sun and well-drained, fertile soil, tying the long canes to their support as they grow since Blaze climbs by producing long stems rather than by twining.

directions: Released in 1932, Blaze is the original large-flowered climber that later gave rise to the better-repeating sport sold as 'Blaze Improved,' and it carries the same clusters of bright, semi-double scarlet-red flowers with a light fragrance on long, vigorous canes capable of covering a substantial fence or arbor. The original form concentrates most of its bloom into one heavy spring flush, with only scattered, lighter rebloom through summer, so gardeners who want the more continuous color of the sport should look for plants specifically labeled 'Improved.' It is an exceptionally tough, cold-hardy, and forgiving climber that tolerates average soil and minimal spray care, which is why it became one of the most widely planted climbing roses in mid-20th-century America. Train canes as horizontally as practical along the support to encourage flowering laterals, and remove only the oldest, least productive canes at the base every couple of years to keep the plant renewing itself.
